scenarioName: Hypoglycemia Masked by Alcohol — Combative Diabetic, IV Dextrose First-Line

scenarioStory.history: 42-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes on insulin. He spent the afternoon watching the Packers game and drinking beer — his wife estimates four or five over about four hours — and skipped dinner entirely. He took his usual evening long-acting insulin around 17:00 before the game. Roughly 40 minutes ago, shortly after the game ended, he began slurring his words, staring blankly, and dropping his phone repeatedly. He became combative and swore at his wife when she tried to get him up off the couch. His 12-year-old daughter, frightened by how he was acting, called 911 from the upstairs bathroom. His wife did not want EMS called and states repeatedly that he is 'just drunk' and 'always gets like this.' The daughter says this is NOT how he normally acts when he drinks — 'he gets quiet and falls asleep, he doesn't get like this.' His skin is cool and soaked with sweat despite a warm house, which does not fit alcohol intoxication.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: A 42-year-old diabetic man who reeks of beer, slurs, sweats, and swings at anyone who touches him. Every surface cue on this scene says 'drunk,' and a dismissive spouse is standing in the doorway confirming it for free. He is hypoglycemic at 42 mg/dL, and the ONLY way the crew finds that out is by putting a glucometer on him. This is not a subtle protocol point — MATC's Hypoglycemia guideline explicitly lists 'patients with suspected alcohol ingestion' and 'patients who appear to be intoxicated' as INCLUSION criteria. The smell of alcohol is a reason to check a sugar, not a reason to skip one. The cool, diaphoretic skin is the physical tell that does not belong to intoxication. His combativeness is not belligerence — MATC states plainly that hypoglycemic patients can be irritable and violent. And the wife's refusal is legally irrelevant: this patient has impaired decision-making capacity, which is the entry criterion for the Altered Mental Status guideline, and an altered patient cannot refuse care through a proxy who is not his guardian. → IV D10 given: Incremental D10% brings him back. Within a few minutes of the first 100–150 mL he stops swinging, opens his eyes, and asks what everyone is doing in his living room. Repeat glucose is 118 mg/dL and his mental status is fully normal — he is oriented, apologetic, and embarrassed. The diaphoresis dries up. Now comes the part crews get wrong: he feels fine, his wife is telling him he doesn't need to go, and he is a competent adult again with every right to refuse. MATC does allow release without transport after hypoglycemia — but it gates it behind EIGHT criteria that must ALL be true, and this patient fails at least two of them outright. He has a major co-morbid symptom (intoxication) and his hypoglycemia was caused by long-acting insulin plus alcohol plus a skipped meal, which will keep working on him for hours after the dextrose wears off. The protocol does not ask the crew how they feel about it; it gives them a checklist, and the checklist says transport.

patientInformation.patientCondition: Confused, slurring his words, and combative when touched. Family says he has been 'acting weird and scary' since the football game ended about 40 minutes ago.

relatedChecklist: CHECK BLOOD GLUCOSE — 'appears intoxicated' is an inclusion criterion, not an exclusion
Work the AEIOU-TIPS differential — do not anchor on alcohol
Recognize combativeness as hypoglycemia, not belligerence; approach safely with a partner
WITHHOLD oral glucose — reserved for a conscious patient with a patent airway; he cannot safely swallow
IV access, then D10% incrementally to max field dose 25 g (250 mL of D10) until mental status improves
Protect the airway — position, suction ready; escalate if he decompensates further
Patient has impaired decision-making capacity — the wife's refusal does not bind you
Full AMS workup: pupils, stroke screen, SpO2/EtCO2, cardiac monitor, breath odor, scan the scene

relatedChecklist: Reassess vitals and mental status post-dextrose; repeat BGM not required once mentation is normal
Apply the 8 release criteria — he FAILS (intoxication); transport is indicated
Transport to closest appropriate facility — hypoglycemia with an identified ongoing driver
Document glucose value, dose/route given, and mental status before AND after treatment

scenarioEvents.name: IV failed — Glucagon given
scenarioEvents.description: This is a CORRECT path, not an error — and it is the one place MATC authorizes glucagon. The patient is thrashing and soaked in sweat, his veins are flat, and two IV attempts have failed. MATC lists glucagon IM/IN explicitly as 'an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established' — a fallback, not a first choice. Adult dose is 1 mg IM/IN. The crew must understand what they have bought: glucagon does not deliver glucose, it tells the liver to release stored glycogen. Onset is slow (10–15 minutes) compared to IV dextrose, and this patient has been drinking heavily on an empty stomach for hours — the population in whom hepatic glycogen stores are most likely to be depleted. So the crew gives the glucagon AND keeps working the access problem, because if he does not wake up, the answer is a line and dextrose, not a second dose of hope. The protocol's own fallback ladder ends with disabling an insulin pump if the above cannot be completed — not applicable here, since he is on injected glargine.
relatedChecklist: Glucagon 1 mg IM/IN (adult fixed dose) — authorized because IV access cannot be established
Keep pursuing vascular access — if he does not wake, the answer is dextrose, not a second glucagon
Reassess mental status and repeat BGM — glucagon onset is slow; do not assume it worked
Protect the airway during the 10–15 min glucagon window — position, suction, monitor
Transport — refractory or slow-to-correct hypoglycemia goes to the ED regardless

scenarioEvents.name: BGM never checked; treated as intoxication
scenarioEvents.description: The crew took the smell of beer, the empty cans, and the wife's word, and never put a glucometer on him. Twenty minutes later the sugar is 31 mg/dL and he is no longer combative — because he is no longer conscious. He is GCS 3 with snoring respirations as his tongue falls back, his rate has dropped to 6, and he is bradycardic and hypoxic from hypoventilation. This is what an untreated hypoglycemic brain does: it stops. The lesson is not subtle and it is not really about diabetes — it is about what happens when a crew lets a plausible story do the work of an assessment. Note that the wife's version of events never changed; she was wrong the whole time, confidently, and the only thing that could ever have corrected her was a $0.30 test strip. The rescue is airway first, then the sugar he should have had twenty minutes ago.
relatedChecklist: AIRWAY FIRST — reposition, suction, OPA (no gag); BVM at 10–12/min for RR 6
Check the blood glucose NOW — the assessment that was owed 20 minutes ago
IV D10% incrementally to max field dose 25 g (250 mL) — unconscious, cannot protect airway
Reassess mental status and vitals; transport — this patient is not a release candidate
Debrief the anchoring error: 'appears intoxicated' is an INCLUSION criterion for this protocol
